newsitem.title: USA: Debate performance yields new and improved Dole.
newsitem.headline: Debate performance yields new and improved Dole.

text.p: For a while, Bob Dole seemed to have disappeared from the public's radar screen.

It was the incredible shrinking campaign, an isolated candidate way behind in the polls, sitting on his plane staring straight ahead while aides scurried around trying to figure out which states were worth fighting for.

Now, invigorated by his Sunday night debate with President Bill Clinton and with the calendar shouting that time is running out before the Nov. 5 election, the Republican presidential candidate seems more ready to do battle. He even wants to do the Oprah Winfrey show.

His steps have a renewed spring, his jokes are sharper and more frequent and his campaign plane, which once seemed like a citadel of silence and suppressed pessimism, is filling with policy advisers and even has a travelling chief of staff.

After bringing his campaign to a near-halt to prepare for the debate -- an event he likened to climbing a mountain -- Dole is back on the trail putting in the 12-to-15 hour days a candidate needs to get noticed.
In New York on Monday night for a TV interview, Dole could not suppress a desire to shake every hand and even to walk up to the window of a restaurant and wave at startled diners.

Staff members, friends and Republican party leaders say the real Bob Dole has finally emerged -- "the warm, witty, compassionate man that Americans can trust to keep his word," according to Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge.
But it is eight days into October and the question is, is it too late?

Polling experts say no presidential candidate has ever been 15 to 20 points behind this late in the campaign and managed to win, although in 1976 Gerald Ford came back from a 30-point deficit to lose to Jimmy Carter by only 1.5 points.

At an Italian-American dinner in Washington on Saturday, that thought was clearly on Dole's mind as he took to the podium to praise former New York Yankees all-star catcher Yogi Berra, "the first man to say, 'It ain't over till it's over.'"

And it was clearly still on his mind at the first stop of his two-day bus tour of New Jersey on Monday. "Don't believe the pundits, don't believe the polls. As (his vice presidential running mate) Jack Kemp says, 'Don't look at the scoreboard when the game is still on.' We are going to win this election," Dole told several thousand supporters at a high school in Toms River.
The audience was enthusiastic. The only problem was they seemed to be mostly pom-pom waving cheerleaders too young to vote.
Some political experts say the first task before Dole is to upgrade his campaign image from that a loser to that of an underdog. The old adage is that Americans hate a loser but love an underdog.
The second step is to cut Clinton's lead in the polls from double to single digits.

His campaign chairman, Scott Reed, said, "I think by the end of the week we'll be back in the high single digits." He said the campaign's internal polls show Dole down about 11 or 12 points nationally with the party's base of support in Southern and Western states now coming home.

A tracking poll of 900 people for Reuters by the Zogby Group International suggested on Tuesday that Dole had closed the gap to just 5.3 points behind Clinton. But tracking polls are subject to extreme fluctuations.

A third step is to convince voters that they should fire Clinton, who is currently presiding over a country that is prosperous and at peace. Dole's chief issue is a promise to enact a 15 percent tax cut, which Clinton says will simply add to the budget deficit.

Dole, who spent years as a deficit hawk, has had trouble convincing people that his plan will work or that he believes in it. During his debate with Clinton, the president went unchallenged as he repeatedly called Dole's plan "a scheme."
But Dole hopes his campaign speech mantra of "It's your money, it's your money, it's your money" will register with voters.
